It is one continuous transformation of a single material, never two separate panels.

The background is the first stack layer, flat and completely empty, and it covers at least forty percent of the picture. There is no circus anywhere: no big top tent, no striped canvas, no spotlight, no poles, no audience, no trapeze bar, no swinging ropes. Only the line, the walker, the net, the pages and the floor.

Upper half. A taut tightrope line, a single straight strip of paper in the primary figure tone, runs perfectly horizontal across the whole picture at about one third of the way down, entering at the left edge and leaving at the right edge. It is firm, not a hairline: about one hundredth of the picture height thick, so it still reads at thumbnail size. Standing on it at the exact horizontal centre is the faceless tightrope walker, a flat paper figure in the primary figure tone, seen in profile, tall enough to fill roughly a quarter of the picture height, from just below the top margin down to the line. His arms are stretched out straight to both sides, level with his shoulders. One foot is placed in front of the other, walking, calm and upright, never falling, never afraid. He wears soft thin-soled slippers, cut as part of the same silhouette, and his front foot rests lengthwise along the line from toe to heel. His hands hold nothing. The head is a smooth plain shape with no face and no features.

Lower half. Below the line, separated from it by a clear band of empty background, a diamond-mesh safety net unraveling into loose pages hangs across the picture from edge to edge, between about four tenths and a half of the way down. The mesh is a lattice of paper strips crossing at 45 degrees, forming even diamonds, in the secondary figure tone. Its two outer stretches, on the left third and on the right third, are whole and tidy, edged along top and bottom by a thicker perimeter rope in the same secondary figure tone that runs out through the side edges of the frame. Moving toward the centre the net changes gradually, one diamond at a time, with no seam and no dividing line: the diamonds loosen and widen, some strips snap and hang as loose cut strand ends with their tips cut at 45 degrees, pointing down toward the pages, the perimeter rope breaks off too, and the openings straighten from diamonds into upright rectangles. Exactly beneath the walker's feet the last rectangles have become sheets of paper. Net and pages are the very same paper in the very same secondary figure tone, simply changing shape.

Focal point. At the centre of the picture, just under the middle and directly below the walker, the last knot of the net, where the tip of the final diamond becomes the upper corner of the first page, is a single accent knot: one small square tie of paper in the accent tone. The accent appears there and nowhere else.

From that knot a staggered column of loose pages seen from the front descends to the floor, held in the middle third of the picture. Each page is an upright rectangle seen flat-on, face toward us, and they sit stacked on top of one another like bricks laid unevenly: each page shifted a little left or a little right of the one above, some taller, some shorter, meeting at right angles with mismatched joints, so the gaps between them form a stepped, irregular vertical path down the column, never a regular grid. Everything is cut paper: hard straight edges and 45-degree cuts, each shape one uniform flat tone, layers read by overlap alone, with no volume and no shine.
